claims.text: Overall tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by competition between mechanical removal of a passive oxide layer and its re-formation by selective oxidation.
Micro-galvanic interactions between phases or compositional regions localize and accelerate corrosion where wear disrupts the passive layer.
The proposed alloy has a nearly homogeneous single-phase or dual-phase microstructure.
The alloy can form a coherent, self-healing passive oxide enriched in selected or noble elements.
Different phases or compositional regions in the alloy have different Volta potentials.
The proposed test applies sliding wear in an aggressive electrolyte, such as 3.5 wt% NaCl, so that the protective film is periodically damaged or removed.
Specimens with identical bulk chemistry but different surface oxidation states or phase distributions can be compared under identical tribological conditions.
Selective development of a passive oxide on one phase rather than another creates local galvanic cells that modulate corrosion rates.
Tribological contact continuously removes the protective passive film.
Removal of the passive film exposes the substrate and accelerates corrosion.
Composition-driven selective oxidation rapidly reforms the passive film after wear damage.
Micro-galvanic coupling between phases with different electrochemical potentials can intensify localized corrosion.
An HEA with a more stable and rapidly re-passivating oxide will have lower total degradation than a baseline with a less robust passive layer.
In the controlled comparison, the wear component may remain similar between the enhanced-passivation specimen and the baseline.
Enhanced re-passivation will reduce the corrosion component and therefore reduce coupled tribo-corrosion degradation.
A brittle passive film or re-passivation slower than film removal can exacerbate both wear and corrosion degradation.
The prediction should hold when the environment is corrosive but oxidation kinetics can keep pace with mechanical film removal.
The prediction may fail under extreme mechanical stress or low oxygen partial pressure that suppresses re-oxidation.
The quantitative balance between film removal and re-passivation and the microscale role of galvanic coupling are not fully quantified by current studies.
Failure of enhanced passivation to significantly reduce corrosion, or failure of Volta-potential differences to correlate with localized corrosion, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
